## Question 1

### 1. Virmati's education, her family's attitude toward educating daughters versus arranging marriage, and the family's sequence of responses (arranged match, confinement/locking up, exile or ostracism)

* Author: Christopher Rollason — Rollason describes Virmati as "an educated woman" who seeks human relations that will allow her to be herself and exercise the control over her life that she knows she deserves (Rollason 1).
* Author: Christopher Rollason — Rollason reports that after rebelling against an arranged marriage, "Insisting on her right to be educated, she manages to leave home to study in Lahore" (Rollason 1).
* Author: Christopher Rollason — Rollason notes that Virmati later works as a school principal and headmistress of a school for girls in Nahan, the capital of the Himalayan state of Sirmaur, where her teaching earns her deserved respect before the Professor's clandestine visits cost her employers' confidence and force her to leave her school, house, and employment (Rollason).
* Author: Christopher Rollason — Rollason observes that after Nahan, Virmati also has the option of going to Shantiniketan, the seat of Rabindranath Tagore's Viswa-Bharati where women were accepted in the educational process, though she never completes the journey after stopping in Delhi (Rollason).
* Author: Christopher Rollason — Rollason writes that after marrying the Professor and returning to Amritsar, "the continuation of her education (she studies for a higher degree in philosophy, but without enthusiasm) feeds no more dreams of independence" (Rollason 3).
* Author: Christopher Rollason — Rollason describes Virmati as "the daughter of a father of progressive ideas and a traditionalist mother (Kasturi, obliged to give birth to no less than 11 children)" who aspires to a freer life than that offered by those around her (Rollason 1).
* Author: Christopher Rollason — Rollason reports that Virmati "is asked to accept a typical arranged marriage" and "rebels against that destiny, to the lasting shame of her family, above all of her mother" (Rollason 1).
* Author: Christopher Rollason — Rollason states that Virmati receives incomprehension from her own family, though any broader discussion of her family's attitude contrasting daughters' education against arranged marriage—beyond her father's progressive ideas, her mother's traditionalism, and Virmati's own insistence on her right to be educated—is not found in the source (Rollason).
* Author: Christopher Rollason — Regarding her family's response after she marries the Professor and returns to Amritsar, Rollason writes that "she ends up being marginalised by her own family and despised by her husband's" (Rollason 1).
* Author: Christopher Rollason — Rollason later summarizes the family's impact as "the psychological annihilation of Virmati, at the hands of her own family and her husband's" (Rollason 4).
* Author: Christopher Rollason — Any report of Virmati's family confining or locking her up, or imposing formal exile or ostracism (beyond the family's lasting shame at her rebellion and her post-marriage marginalisation), is not found in the source (Rollason).

### 2. Power dynamics between Virmati, Harish (the Professor), and Virmati's family elders over her marriage and autonomy

* Author: Christopher Rollason — The name Harish does not appear anywhere in the source; Rollason refers to him only as an Amritsar teacher, a married man, her parents' tenant, her husband, the Professor, the fatal Professor, and the fateful Professor (Rollason).
* Author: Christopher Rollason — Specific references to family elders (or negotiations involving extended elders) over Virmati's marriage and autonomy are not found in the source, which refers instead to her parents, her father of progressive ideas, her traditionalist mother Kasturi, and her own family (Rollason).
* Author: Christopher Rollason — Rollason writes that Virmati challenges her family's expectation when she "is asked to accept a typical arranged marriage," rebels "to the lasting shame of her family, above all of her mother," and leaves home to study in Lahore by "[i]nsisting on her right to be educated" (Rollason 1).
* Author: Christopher Rollason — Wait: to preserve exact verbatim text without bracketed changes, Rollason records that Virmati "rebels against that destiny, to the lasting shame of her family, above all of her mother" and then "Insisting on her right to be educated, she manages to leave home to study in Lahore" (Rollason 1).
* Author: Christopher Rollason — Rollason attributes the failure of Virmati's aspiration for a freer life not only to "the incomprehension she receives from both her own family and that of the man she marries," but also to "her own mistakes, for no-one obliged her to marry who became her husband, and she was free not to make the choice she did" (Rollason 1).
* Author: Christopher Rollason — Rollason notes that Virmati falls in love with "a married man who first appears in her life as her parents' tenant," and that even after she marries him and returns to Amritsar, "he refuses to leave his first wife, and the consequences for Virmati are harsh indeed: she ends up being marginalised by her own family and despised by her husband's" (Rollason 1).
* Author: Christopher Rollason — Rollason observes that in Nahan, Virmati attains "the greatest degree of control over her life" and "a near-exemplary level of female autonomy," yet loses them because "She believes she needs a man, and she makes the wrong choice, returning to a relationship that had already brought her nothing but suffering" (Rollason 2).
* Author: Christopher Rollason — Rollason adds that in Nahan, "The repeated clandestine visits of the fatal Professor lose Virmati her employers' confidence, and she is obliged to quit her school, house and employment" (Rollason 2).
* Author: Christopher Rollason — Rollason notes that Virmati's prospect of "renewed autonomy" at Shantiniketan fades when a long train wait in Delhi "opens up a trap that she falls into: she contacts an acquaintance in the capital, who is also a friend of the fateful Professor" (Rollason 3).
* Author: Christopher Rollason — Rollason writes that in married life with the Professor in Amritsar, Virmati "loses all sense of identity" and her further study "feeds no more dreams of independence" (Rollason 3).
* Author: Christopher Rollason — Rollason states that Virmati chooses "the road that leads to the Professor" over political activism, quoting her own recognition that "'my time is spent being in love'" rather than engaging in activist work like Shakuntala and Swarna (Rollason 4).
* Author: Christopher Rollason — Rollason describes Virmati's outcome as "the psychological annihilation of Virmati, at the hands of her own family and her husband's," while insisting it "should not be read as a fatality" (Rollason 4).
* Author: Christopher Rollason — Rollason quotes Dora Sales Salvador's observation that in the novel, the tension between "the weight of gender-determined tradition" and "the yearning for independence and self-affirmation" is not a simple dichotomy, but involves "complex emotional shades of grey" (Rollason 4).
* Author: Christopher Rollason — Rollason quotes Dora Sales's statement that Virmati "'could not speak out, being certainly situated at the juncture of two oppressions: colonialism and patriarchy'" (Rollason 5).
* Author: Christopher Rollason — Rollason also cites Gur Pyari Jandial's view on Virmati's effort against patriarchal authority: "'What is necessary is to break the patriarchal mould, and for Virmati to have tried to do that in the forties was a great achievement'" (Rollason 5).

* Author: Christopher Rollason — Rollason notes that the Professor refuses to leave his first wife and that Virmati ends up despised by her husband's family and subjected to psychological annihilation at the hands of both her own family and her husband's (Rollason).
* Author: Christopher Rollason — Specific details regarding Ganga's domestic authority, daily routine, or silence (as well as the name Harish, or any further particulars of Ganga's treatment of Virmati beyond her implacable and hostile gaze) are not found in the source (Rollason).

## Question 2

### 1. Virmati's pregnancy episode—exact term used (abortion, miscarriage, etc.) and secrecy, silence, or who knows

* Author: Christopher Rollason — Rollason does not mention or describe any pregnancy episode involving Virmati anywhere in the essay, and no terms such as abortion, miscarriage, or pregnancy in connection with Virmati appear in the source (Rollason).
* Author: Christopher Rollason — Because no pregnancy episode is mentioned, details about secrecy, silence, or who knows regarding such an episode are not found in the source (Rollason).
* Author: Christopher Rollason — The only mentions in the essay of clandestine behavior, avoiding open scandal, or Virmati's inability to speak out refer respectively to the Professor's clandestine visits to Nahan, Virmati's pretext of Shantiniketan with her employers, and Dora Sales's comment on Virmati's lack of voice under colonialism and patriarchy—none of which concern a pregnancy episode (Rollason).

### 2. Ida's framing narration, Ida's reconstruction of her mother's silent/absent past, and how Partition is represented (or fragmented/indirectly told) in *Difficult Daughters*

* Author: Christopher Rollason — Rollason explains that "Virmati's tale is told, from a present-day perspective, by Ida, her only daughter, who seeks to reconstruct her late mother's life-story, against the background of the Independence movement of the 1940s and the subsequent trauma of Partition" (Rollason 1).
* Author: Christopher Rollason — Rollason notes regarding the narrative structure: "*Difficult Daughters* is not a pure third-person narrative. Virmati's story is told mostly in the third person (with some recourse to the epistolary mode)" (Rollason 4).
* Author: Christopher Rollason — Rollason adds that this third-person account is framed by the first-person narration of a search: "The search is that of Virmati's daughter, Ida, as she seeks to reconstitute her mother's history" (Rollason 5).
* Author: Christopher Rollason — Rollason characterizes Ida as "an educated woman, divorced and childless" who "apparently leads a freer life than her mother's in external terms" while still feeling internally "some of the same anxieties as had plagued her mother," quoting Ida's words: "'No matter how I might rationalize otherwise, I feel my existence as a single woman reverberate desolately'" (Rollason 5).
* Author: Christopher Rollason — Rollason states that Ida, "the narrator through whose voice Kapur speaks, has achieved more than her mother (and much more than her grandmother): and that this is so even through the simple creative fact of 'writing down' her own family history," representing "a qualitative leap between the life-histories of (narrated) mother and (narrating) daughter" (Rollason 5).
* Author: Christopher Rollason — Regarding Virmati's silence and Ida's reconstruction, Rollason quotes Dora Sales Salvador: "'In *Difficult Daughters* we do not listen to Virmati's voice. She could not speak out, being certainly situated at the juncture of two oppressions: colonialism and patriarchy. What we have is her daughter's reconstruction and representation'" (Rollason 5).
* Author: Christopher Rollason — Beyond stating that Ida seeks to reconstruct and reconstitute her late mother's history by writing down her family history and citing Dora Sales on Virmati's inability to speak out, Rollason does not analyze specific mechanisms of narrative absence, gaps, or silent family memories (Rollason).
* Author: Christopher Rollason — Regarding Partition's thematic role, Rollason writes that the novel's search for control over one's destiny "refers to the Independence aspired to and obtained by a nation (despite its cruel division by a fateful Partition), but also to the independence yearned after (and finally not obtained) by a woman and member of that same nation (or of one of its rival communities)" (Rollason 1).
* Author: Christopher Rollason — Rollason describes the Independence movement of the 1940s and the subsequent trauma of Partition as the historical background against which Ida reconstructs Virmati's life-story, and notes that women participated forcefully in the social movements leading up to Independence and Partition (Rollason).
* Author: Christopher Rollason — Rollason writes that at the conclusion of Virmati's personal narrative in Amritsar, "her individual history disappears and becomes all but irrelevant, swallowed up in the greater and more resonant collective tragedy of Partition" (Rollason 3).
* Author: Christopher Rollason — Any discussion characterizing the representation of Partition in *Difficult Daughters* as fragmented or indirectly told is not found in the source (Rollason).

### 3. Whether Rollason mentions Manju Kapur originally considering calling the novel "Partitions"

* Author: Christopher Rollason — Rollason does not mention anything about Manju Kapur originally considering calling the novel Partitions; this information is not found in the source (Rollason).

### 1. Division Between the Outer/Material Domain and Inner/Spiritual Domain (Home), and Regulation of Women's Conduct, Modesty, and Speech

* Author: Partha Chatterjee — Nationalist ideology resolved its struggle against colonial dominance by dividing culture into two spheres: the material sphere (science, technology, rational economic organization, and modern statecraft), where Western civilization was most powerful and had to be learned, and the spiritual sphere, where the East considered itself superior to the West and sought to preserve its distinctive essence (Chatterjee).
* Author: Partha Chatterjee — Chatterjee explains that nationalist ideology condensed this material and spiritual distinction into an even more powerful spatial and ideological binary: "The discourse of nationalism shows that the material/spiritual distinction was condensed into an analogous, but ideologically far more powerful, dichotomy: that between the outer and the inner" (Chatterjee 624).
* Author: Partha Chatterjee — Chatterjee summarizes how nationalist writers viewed the outer material realm in relation to the inner spiritual core: "The material domain, argued nationalist writers, lies outside us—a mere external, which influences us, conditions us, and to which we are forced to adjust. But ultimately it is unimportant. It is the spiritual, which lies within, that is our true self; it is that which is genuinely essential" (Chatterjee 624).
* Author: Partha Chatterjee — Chatterjee describes how this inner/outer dichotomy separated everyday social space and assigned gendered roles: "Applying the inner/outer distinction to the matter of concrete day-to-day living separates the social space into *ghar* and *bāhir*, the home and the world. The world is the external, the domain of the material; the home represents one’s inner spiritual self, one’s true identity. The world is a treacherous terrain of the pursuit of material interests, where practical considerations reign supreme. It is also typically the domain of the male. The home in its essence must remain unaffected by the profane activities of the material world—and woman is its representation. And so one gets an identification of social roles by gender to correspond with the separation of the social space into *ghar* and *bāhir*" (Chatterjee 624).
* Author: Partha Chatterjee — Nationalists argued that although European powers had subjugated colonized peoples in the material world—forcing them to learn Western sciences and accept colonial norms there in order to eventually overthrow colonial rule—colonialism had failed to colonize the East's sovereign spiritual identity, making it crucial to prevent any colonial encroachment inside the inner sanctum (Chatterjee).
* Author: Partha Chatterjee — Chatterjee highlights the sharp contrast between what was required in public versus inside the home: "In the world, imitation of and adaptation to Western norms was a necessity: at home, they were tantamount to annihilation of one’s very identity" (Chatterjee 624–625).
* Author: Partha Chatterjee — Because external social changes entangled the family and forced men to make compromises in their dress, food habits, religious observances, and social relations, women at home were tasked with preserving indigenous spirituality to compensate for men's material surrenders (Chatterjee).
* Author: Partha Chatterjee — Chatterjee states why the home became the primary site for safeguarding women's conduct and virtues: "The home was the principal site for expressing the spiritual quality of the national culture, and women must take the main responsibility for protecting and nurturing this quality. No matter what the changes in the external conditions of life for women, they must not lose their essentially spiritual (that is, feminine) virtues; they must not, in other words, become essentially Westernized" (Chatterjee 626–627).
* Author: Partha Chatterjee — Chatterjee details the compensatory behavioral restrictions placed on women to maintain spiritual purity at home: "They must not eat, drink or smoke in the same way as men; they must continue the observance of religious rituals which men were finding difficult to carry out; they must maintain the cohesiveness of family life and solidarity with the kin to which men could not now devote much attention" (Chatterjee 629).

### Question 2

#### 1. How Butalia describes the fragmented, second-hand manner in which Partition stories and women's histories reach later generations through relatives' memories and oral accounts

- Author: Urvashi Butalia — Raised in a Punjabi refugee family from Lahore, Butalia grew up hearing constant stories of Partition horror alongside nostalgic recollections of pre-Partition harmony, yet she and her siblings barely absorbed them until the 1984 anti-Sikh violence forced her to recognize how Partition continued to shape family life (Butalia).
- Author: Urvashi Butalia — Reflecting on her childhood indifference to relatives' Partition stories, Butalia writes: "I would listen to these stories with my brothers and sister and hardly take them in. We were middle-class Indians who had grown up in a period of relative calm and prosperity, when tolerance and 'secularism' seemed to be winning the argument. These stories — of loot, arson, rape, murder — came out of a different time. They meant little to me." (Butalia 4).
- Author: Urvashi Butalia — Describing how tales of women's deaths first reached her indirectly, Butalia states: "Many were horrific and of a kind that, when I was younger and heard them second or third hand, I had found hard to believe: women jumping into wells to drown themselves so as to avoid rape or forced religious conversion; fathers beheading their own children so they would avoid the same dishonourable fate. Now I was hearing them from witnesses whose bitterness, rage and hatred — which, once uncovered, could be frightening — told me they were speaking the truth." (Butalia 5).
- Author: Urvashi Butalia — Explaining why her generation initially dismissed family stories that clashed with formal education, Butalia writes: "In many ways I began as an innocent: someone familiar with the 'history' of the event — as many Indians are who have to study 'modern history' at school — and someone who had grown up on stories of it, stories that somehow did not match what we learnt at school, stories that, perhaps because of that, we discounted." (Butalia 347).
- Author: Urvashi Butalia — On the fragility of Partition recall outside public institutions, Butalia observes: "Refugee camps became part of the landscape of most major cities in the north, but, a half century later, there is still no memorial, no memory, no recall, except what is guarded, and now rapidly dying, in families and collective memory." (Butalia 45).
- Author: Urvashi Butalia — Questioning how second- and third-generation descendants inherit divisive attitudes without direct experience of 1947, Butalia writes: "Why is it that so many second and third generation Hindus and Sikhs after Partition have come to internalize notions of 'us' and 'them' when they have no reference of Partition — except through family and community memories? What is it about the selectivity of memory that, in this case, feelings of fear and hatred seem to have been nurtured, to have a greater resilience, while feelings of friendship and sharing are not allowed to surface?" (Butalia 12).
- Author: Urvashi Butalia — Describing how women's histories emerged only gradually rather than through direct historical records, Butalia states: "I cannot now pinpoint exactly when I became aware of the histories of women. I say 'became aware' because the process was a sort of cumulative one, where stories began to seep into my consciousness until one day when it became clear that there was something I should be actively seeking." (Butalia 125).
- Author: Urvashi Butalia — Describing the interrupted, non-linear structure of household interviews across generations, Butalia writes: "Most conversations took place in family situations: even though we may have been speaking to one person, the entire family — often several generations of it — would converge, and every now and again, someone or the other would offer an explanation, or take on a question. Stories begun would be left incomplete, and when resumed, would move on to something else. Later, we might come back to the same story, or not at all. No neat chronologies marked the telling; there were no clear beginnings and endings." (Butalia 23).
- Author: Urvashi Butalia — Relatives and survivors frequently blurred temporal boundaries when recalling trauma, merging 1947 and 1984 together so that remembering meant reliving the past through the present, while speakers broke off mid-sentence when memories became too painful to articulate (Butalia).
- Author: Urvashi Butalia — Noting a paradox in how older relatives talk about Partition, Butalia observes: "People of my parents' generation tell stories of Partition all the time: it preoccupies their minds, it fills their lives, it memorializes their pasts. Yet when you sit them down, formally, as if to interview them about these very stories, they are strangely reluctant to talk." (Butalia 53).
- Author: Urvashi Butalia — Reflecting on how little close relatives sometimes knew about a woman's Partition ordeal—such as Damyanti Sahgal's sister Kamla and niece Lina hearing Damyanti's stories for the first time during Butalia's interviews—Butalia writes: "Even for her sister and niece, the experiences she recounted were new. At one point Kamla asked Damyanti why she had never told these stories before. Listening to them, I found it difficult to believe that even in the closest of relationships in families, people could be so ignorant of — and indifferent to — what was going on in the life of someone so close to them." (Butalia 113).
- Author: Urvashi Butalia — Within Butalia's own family, her mother and aunts only learned forty years after Partition that their mother Dayawanti had converted, taken a Muslim name, and lived until 1956 before being buried in Lahore, when Butalia travelled to Pakistan to visit her uncle Ranamama and brought back his letters and news (Butalia).
- Author: Urvashi Butalia — In community remembrance ceremonies like Shahidi Diwas in Jangpura, stories of women's martyrdom are transmitted across a widening generational divide from dwindling numbers of elders to rapt children and young people, while younger generations inside families such as Mangal Singh's or Rajinder Singh's often dismissed or ignored elders' accounts until external interest or tape recordings lent them authority (Butalia).
- Author: Urvashi Butalia — Observing the growing distance between original witnesses and younger listeners at community rituals, Butalia writes: "Over the years as the number of the survivors of Rawalpindi has decreased, the gap between the teller of the stories and the audience has increased: young people and small children now sit in the audience, listening, often rapt, for the stories are told with skill and passion." (Butalia 364).
- Author: Urvashi Butalia — Because women who experienced rape and abduction rarely spoke directly, women's histories reached later generations indirectly through archival fragments, memoirs delayed for decades like Kamlaben Patel's, or the accounts of social workers like Damyanti Sahgal, and were inevitably mediated when written down by researchers after repeated tellings (Butalia).

#### 2. Observations Butalia makes about what family members leave unsaid, conceal, or speak around when recounting Partition events involving women

- Author: Urvashi Butalia — Because nearly every family had histories of being both victims and aggressors during Partition, families preferred to suppress shameful truths internally rather than remember them publicly, with people partitioning their minds to cast themselves solely as victims and pretend they had not killed (Butalia).
- Author: Urvashi Butalia — Explaining why families kept unpleasant parts of Partition history hidden from public view, Butalia writes: "surely that told us something about why people did not wish to remember it, publicly, except perhaps within their families where the 'ugly' parts of this history could be suppressed." (Butalia 11).
- Author: Urvashi Butalia — Identifying two distinct forms of family concealment, Butalia states: "I began to understand, gradually, that the silences of Partition are of many kinds. If, at one level, we are faced with a kind of historical silence, at another this is compounded by a familial silence, in which families have colluded in hiding their own histories, sometimes actively as the two brothers I met in Jangpura had done, and sometimes simply through indifference, as had happened, to some extent, in my own family." (Butalia 358-59).
- Author: Urvashi Butalia — Re-examining her interviews after noticing families never mentioned rape or abduction, Butalia writes: "Why had they made no mention of the rape and abduction of women? Were these deliberate erasures or could it be that I had asked the wrong questions? Or simply not listened to the nuance, the half-said things? I thought, perhaps I had missed out something, perhaps people had talked about this. So I went back over my interviews. And, suddenly, there it was, in the odd silence, the ambiguous phrase." (Butalia 133).
- Author: Urvashi Butalia — In the case of the two Rawalpindi brothers in Delhi, their declaration that all their family had been killed concealed the disappearance of their two abducted sisters, whom neighbours only referred to indirectly in ashamed whispers (Butalia).
- Author: Urvashi Butalia — Describing how male relatives dominated family interviews and silenced women, Butalia observes: "Equally, if their husbands or sons were around, they tended to take over the interview, inadvertently or otherwise, making women lapse into a sort of silence." (Butalia 15).
- Author: Urvashi Butalia — Explaining how family fears kept women deferring to men in joint interviews, Butalia writes: "In joint interviews — and because Partition is so much a part of 'family' histories, and also because families are often fearful of 'letting' their members speak about Partition without the elders, usually the men, being around — it was always the men who spoke. If addressed directly, the women would defer to the men." (Butalia 353).
- Author: Urvashi Butalia — On the need to listen beyond direct speech when interviewing women, Butalia writes: "many oral historians have written about the difficulty of speaking to and with women, of learning to listen differently, often of listening to the hidden nuance, the half-said thing, the silences which are sometimes more eloquent than speech." (Butalia 16).
- Author: Urvashi Butalia — Noting how both men and women marginalized women's own experiences in conversation, Butalia states: "The men seldom spoke about women. Women almost never spoke about themselves, indeed they denied they had anything 'worthwhile' to say, a stance that was often corroborated by their men. Or, quite often, they simply weren't there to speak to." (Butalia 126).
- Author: Urvashi Butalia — Even when interviewed apart from men, women often began by claiming they had nothing important to say and tailored their stories to what they believed the interviewer or their men wanted to hear, using dominant male-framed concepts that muted their immediate experiences unless the listener tuned into both dominant and muted channels (Butalia).
- Author: Urvashi Butalia — Highlighting a sharp gendered difference in what men and women omit when remembering Partition, Butalia writes: "From the women I learned about the minutiae of their lives, while for the most part men spoke of the relations between communities, the broad political realities. Seldom was there an occasion when a man being interviewed would speak of a child lost or killed, while for a woman there was no way in which she could omit such a reference." (Butalia 16).
- Author: Urvashi Butalia — Butalia observes that Bir Bahadur Singh spoke around his mother Basant Kaur's survival at the Thoa Khalsa well while focusing on his sister Maan Kaur's honourable death, and preemptively denied that any women from Thoa Khalsa were listed in the government registry of abducted women so that his family's killings would not appear futile (Butalia).
- Author: Urvashi Butalia — Condemning the dishonest euphemisms families and communities used to speak around violence against women and children, Butalia writes: "So much violence, so much pain and grief, often so much dishonesty about the violence — killing women was not violence, it was saving the honour of the community, losing sight of children, abandoning them to who knew what fate was not violence, it was maintaining the purity of the religion, killing people of the other religion was not murder, it was somehow excusable" (Butalia 359).
- Author: Urvashi Butalia — Observing how martyrdom rhetoric masks coercion inside families, Butalia states: "Instead, such acts are represented, in so much of what we say and do, as valorous acts, shorn of the violence, and indeed coercion, that must have sent so many women to their deaths." (Butalia 214).
- Author: Urvashi Butalia — Explaining how blaming the external enemy obscures internal family violence against women, Butalia writes: "It is for this reason, I feel, that during Partition, and in so much of the recall of Partition, violence is seen as relating only to the 'other'. This obscures the very important fact that many women of Hindu and Sikh communities must have seen the men of their own communities as being perpetrators of violence against them — for just as there were 'voluntary' suicides, there were also mass murders." (Butalia 215).
- Author: Urvashi Butalia — On what heroic community accounts hide about male relatives' actions, Butalia writes: "The women's martyrdom conceals the men's complicity." (Butalia 364).
- Author: Urvashi Butalia — In family and community retellings of Rawalpindi villages like Thoa Khalsa and Thamali, survivors left unmentioned protracted negotiations with attackers, handing over money and weapons, attempts to barter a village woman for peace, women who refused to die, and women who were abducted, remembering only valour in order to forget rape, abduction, and failure to protect (Butalia).
- Author: Urvashi Butalia — Families also kept histories of rape, abduction, and ashram residence concealed from younger relatives, husbands, and children—such as women married through ashrams hiding their pasts or the Jalandhar woman doctor hiding her ashram upbringing from her children—while even Butalia chose to keep parts of her uncle Ranamama's confession silent so as not to expose him to danger (Butalia).

### Question 1

#### 1.1 How Virmati's family initially permits or encourages her education, and at what exact point and for what stated reasons the family begins to regret educating her
- Author: Manju Kapur — Virmati explains to Ganga that women studying is a tradition in her family because her mother and maternal aunt studied, and her father continually brings books and magazines home for her mother to read (Kapur).
- Author: Manju Kapur — Virmati states proudly to Ganga, "My mother, my masi, all studied. It is the rivaz in our family" (Kapur ch. 8).
- Author: Manju Kapur — Virmati recalls that her grandfather always praised female education in the region, noting he said "the women of the Punjab were among the most advanced in the country" (Kapur ch. 8).
- Author: Manju Kapur — Initially, not much attention is paid to Virmati's schooling: as a child she attends the Arya Kanya Mahavidyalaya, and after Class VIII she is sent to Stratford College for classes IX and X and two years for a Fine Arts degree, after which the elders plan her marriage (Kapur).
- Author: Manju Kapur — When Virmati's marriage is postponed by one year after her great-aunt's death and then postponed again after her fiancé's father's death, her grandfather supports her continuing to college for her BA, telling Kasturi, "The girl is serious. It is natural" (Kapur ch. 8).
- Author: Manju Kapur — When Kasturi expresses unease about Virmati studying at AS College alongside four hundred boys and only six other girls, Kasturi seeks reassurance from Ganga, who assures her that Virmati's future is safe there (Kapur).
- Author: Manju Kapur — Suraj Prakash later explains to the Diwan of Sirmaur that families educate daughters to match educated sons, stating, "With the boys becoming educated, and often opting for professional careers, there is the need for girls to keep up with them. Otherwise, where is the compatibility?" (Kapur ch. 21).
- Author: Manju Kapur — The family's regret begins when Virmati finishes her BA, asks Kasturi to delay her fixed wedding, suggests Indumati marry instead, and says she wants to go to Lahore to study, prompting Kasturi to bang Virmati's head against the wall (Kapur).
- Author: Manju Kapur — At this initial confrontation in Chapter 10, Kasturi reflects with stated regret on what education has done to her daughter: "What kind of learning was this, that deprived her of her reason? She too knew the value of education, it had got her her husband, and had filled her hours with the pleasure of reading. In her time, going to school had been a privilege, not to be abused by going against one's parents" (Kapur ch. 10).
- Author: Manju Kapur — Immediately after Virmati's suicide attempt at Tarsikka and her return home, the family collectively condemns her education when she says she wants to study, questioning, "Was this all her education had taught her? To put herself before others, and damn the rest?" (Kapur ch. 13).
- Author: Manju Kapur — At that same interrogation, Kasturi slaps Virmati across both cheeks and exclaims, "For this, I let you go to college. So that you are ruined permanently? Are you mad?" (Kapur ch. 13).
- Author: Manju Kapur — Lajwanti blames an outside corrupting influence on Virmati's studies, asserting that someone has been teaching her because otherwise Virmati is not the academic type, and Kasturi agrees that Virmati has learned how to run away and throw herself in a canal (Kapur).
- Author: Manju Kapur — While Virmati is confined in the godown, she writes to Harish that Kasturi blames college for her defiance, wishes she had married after Inter, and accuses her of thinking she knows more than her parents and giving a setback to the Arya Samaj effort to educate girls (Kapur).
- Author: Manju Kapur — Later, while confined on the terrace, Virmati writes to Harish, "My mother keeps saying that all my education has achieved is the destruction of my family" (Kapur ch. 14).
- Author: Manju Kapur — When Kasturi takes Virmati to Lahore for her BT, she treats further study as a mere fallback after Virmati ruined her marriage prospects and complains that whereas eighth-class pass satisfied her own generation, Virmati thinks she is too special to follow family ways (Kapur).
- Author: Manju Kapur — When the Diwan of Sirmaur praises Virmati's qualifications, Kasturi privately thinks "how disastrously educating Virmati had misfired" and later tells Suraj Prakash that all that studying harmed Virmati's health and left her past listening to anyone (Kapur ch. 21).
- Author: Manju Kapur — After Virmati marries Harish without consent and visits her natal home, Kasturi mocks her education while throwing her out: "But no! You were too conceited to listen to anybody – why should you? – you are so educated, aren't you?" (Kapur ch. 23).
- Author: Manju Kapur — Years later, Suraj Prakash also reflects with grief on how education estranged his daughter, thinking, "After she had been educated, she had gone her own way, changed from the caring, responsible girl she had always been, to a stranger, deaf to reason, threats or pleading" (Kapur ch. 24).

#### 1.2 How the novel depicts Virmati's relationship with the married Professor (Harish) as unacceptable to her household, and which family members or men speak for or negotiate over Virmati
- Author: Manju Kapur — The relationship is depicted as doubly unacceptable because Virmati is already betrothed to a respectable Arya Samaj boy, Inderjit, and breaking her engagement threatens the marriage prospects of her five younger sisters (Kapur).
- Author: Manju Kapur — While imprisoned in the godown, Virmati writes to Harish that her parents condemn his marital status, telling her, "A man who is already married and a traitor to his wife can never give happiness to any woman. - Author: Manju Kapur — Harish relays through a letter that Ganga reports to him how Virmati's grandfather avoids Amritsar out of shame and how the family considers Virmati to have disgraced them and ruined her sisters' marriage chances (Kapur).
- Author: Manju Kapur — Kasturi regards Harish as a predatory, immoral outsider, telling Suraj Prakash, "He cast an evil eye on her. With simple people such as us, he could do anything! - Author: Manju Kapur — After Virmati marries Harish, Kasturi treats the union as total ruin and moral contamination, shouting at Virmati, "You've destroyed our family, you badmash, you randi! You've blackened our face everywhere!" and ordering her back to "her cheap, dishonoured home!" (Kapur ch. 23).

- Author: Manju Kapur — Enforcing the Inderjit engagement and substituting Indumati is explicitly stated to protect the family's pledged word, its good name, and the marriageability of the remaining five daughters, as Kasturi warns Virmati against wanting them to "break our word and destroy our good name" and asks what face they can show the boy's family (Kapur ch. 10).

- Author: Manju Kapur — Rejecting and ostracizing Virmati after her marriage to Harish protects Kasturi and the remaining family from ongoing association with what Kasturi calls "shame on our family, shame on me, shame on Bade Pitaji!" and preserves the family's moral standing in the community (Kapur ch. 23).

#### 2.2 How Ganga (the first wife) responds to Virmati's arrival and presence
- Author: Manju Kapur — At the moment Virmati arrives at Moti Cottage, Ganga's eyes fill with tears and she stumbles inside, soon cutting vegetables in the kitchen while wishing to slash her own throat so the new bride would slip in the blood and break her head (Kapur).

- Author: Manju Kapur — When Virmati tries to cook for herself, Ganga defends her domestic monopoly through dramatic purification: "there had been such weeping and wailing that day, such ritual rinsing of every pot and pan to wash away her polluted touch, that she felt intimidated. - Author: Manju Kapur — Ganga responds with hostile physical looks and intense gazes: near the pump she looks fixedly away while "viciously spitting out bits of the neem twig she was using to clean her teeth" (Kapur ch. 23).
- Author: Manju Kapur — Whenever Ganga sees Virmati, "she would turn her face away, or what was worse, would stare intensely at her, her eyes moist, her lip trembling, her big red bindi flashing accusingly" (Kapur ch. 23).

- Author: Manju Kapur — Even when forced to evacuate to Kanpur during the 1946–47 communal disturbances, Ganga leaves her big steel almirah locked to assert her continuing claim on the household and promise her eventual return (Kapur).

#### 2.3 Textual evidence showing whether Ganga's domestic routine and silence function as resistance against Harish and Virmati, complicity with patriarchal household norms, or both
- Author: Manju Kapur — The text provides direct evidence that Ganga's domestic routine and silence function as both resistance against Virmati (and indirectly Harish) and complicity with patriarchal household norms (Kapur).
- Author: Manju Kapur — Functioning as resistance, Ganga treats the kitchen and household labour as territory she refuses to surrender ("If Virmati had the bed, Ganga was going to have the house"), driving Virmati out with weeping and ritual cleansing of Virmati's "polluted touch" (Kapur ch. 23).
- Author: Manju Kapur — Functioning as resistance against Virmati's displacement of her, Ganga engages in covert domestic sabotage—ruining Virmati's lassi and food, leaving her clothes in the rain, cutting off her access to the children, and locking her steel almirah in 1947 as "a lock that asserted her claims, and promised she would return" (Kapur ch. 26).
- Author: Manju Kapur — Functioning as emotional resistance and leverage inside the household, Ganga uses silence, hostile staring, loud self-pitying prayers for death within Virmati's earshot (making Virmati feel "like a murderess"), and silent resentment of Harish's Lahore visits so that Harish feels pressured at home (Kapur ch. 23).
- Author: Manju Kapur — Ganga explicitly resolves never to surrender her place in the marriage, thinking after Virmati leaves for Lahore, "She herself would never clear the field for anyone" (Kapur ch. 25).
- Author: Manju Kapur — Simultaneously functioning as complicity with patriarchal household norms, Ganga accepts Kishori Devi's admonition that a woman must simply perform duty, serve elders, and accept her predetermined lot without rebelling against her husband directly (Kapur).
- Author: Manju Kapur — Rather than confronting Harish for taking a second wife, Ganga channels her hostility toward Virmati ("the witch"), fasts twice weekly for Harish's long and prosperous life, and hopes Virmati bears a girl rather than a rival son (Kapur ch. 24).
- Author: Manju Kapur — Ganga actively performs submissive wifely devotion to regain Harish's favour while Virmati is in Lahore, pressing his legs every day with "eyes downcast" and looking at him with "abject gratitude" when he gently pulls her mangalsutra out of her blouse (Kapur ch. 25).
- Author: Manju Kapur — Ganga defines her own identity completely within patriarchal marital symbols and domestic service: she resents Virmati because Ganga had dutifully tended house, children, in-laws, and salary, and in the Epilogue, "Her husband continued to be Ganga's public statement of selfhood. Her bindi and her bangles, her toe rings and her man-galsutra, all managed to suggest that he was still her god" (Kapur ch. 27).

#### 2.4 What keeping this household arrangement protects for Harish and Ganga, and what it costs Virmati
- Author: Manju Kapur — For Harish, the arrangement protects both his domestic comfort and his romantic/intellectual desires without extra financial expense, since Kishori Devi knows "he could not afford to keep two separate households" and Harish admits to himself he could not bear living alone with Ganga (Kapur ch. 22).
- Author: Manju Kapur — Harish preserves Ganga's tireless domestic service, hosting of guests, and personal care ("She was so convenient") while keeping Virmati as his sexual and educated "companion," summing up the split explicitly: "Poor thing, you have me, let her have the kitchen" (Kapur ch. 23).
- Author: Manju Kapur — Harish also protects public respectability and harmony with his mother by forcing Virmati to remain quiet at night, avoid demanding special treatment, and appear cheerful before others (Kapur).
- Author: Manju Kapur — For Ganga, keeping this household arrangement protects her authority as mistress of the house and kitchen, her exclusive bond with her children and mother-in-law, her financial security, her public status as a virtuous housewife, and her renewed conjugal intimacy with Harish once Virmati departs for Lahore (Kapur).
- Author: Manju Kapur — For Virmati, the arrangement costs her daily dignity and belonging, reducing her to "a place where her pariah status was announced with every averted look" and subjecting her to the "humiliation of being served before everybody else like a guest" by her mother-in-law (Kapur ch. 23).
- Author: Manju Kapur — It costs Virmati basic domestic autonomy and nourishment, forcing her to bathe last, give up morning milk, forego lassi and meals Harish does not eat, and watch her laundry get rained on and ignored (Kapur).
- Author: Manju Kapur — It costs Virmati emotional warmth and family connection, leaving her isolated from women, rejected by Harish's children who call her "gandi mummy," driven to feel "like a murderess," and driven to petty retaliatory displays using Harish as her "only weapon" (Kapur ch. 23).
- Author: Manju Kapur — Ultimately, it costs Virmati her health, spirit, and academic freedom: after Kishori Devi sleeps beside her during pregnancy and Virmati suffers a miscarriage, Virmati turns into "a block of wood, whose only response to the world was the passive oozing of tears," and is packed off to Lahore to study philosophy, a subject she hates (Kapur ch. 24).

### Question 3

#### 3.1 Exact word(s) the novel itself uses for what happens to Virmati's premarital pregnancy in Lahore
- Author: Manju Kapur — The novel repeatedly and explicitly uses the exact word "abortion" (and "abortions") for the termination of Virmati's premarital pregnancy in Lahore (Kapur ch. 19).
- Author: Manju Kapur — When Ida talks to the elderly Swarna Lata Sondhi about Virmati's pregnancy in Chapter 19, Ida privately reflects on her own parallel experience, thinking, "I knew, Mother, what it was like to have an abortion" (Kapur ch. 19).
- Author: Manju Kapur — While facing her options in Lahore, the narration states that Virmati "had heard stories of women sometimes bleeding to death after these home-done abortions" (Kapur ch. 19).
- Author: Manju Kapur — Immediately after the procedure in Miss Datta's guest room, during her practical exams, Virmati wonders of the examiner, "could he tell that she had just had an abortion?" (Kapur ch. 19).
- Author: Manju Kapur — At the close of Chapter 19 after returning home to Amritsar, the narration states, "Her body had gone through knives and abortion, what could happen to her now that she could not bear?" (Kapur ch. 19).
- Author: Manju Kapur — Later in the novel, after Virmati's post-marital pregnancy ends involuntarily, the text explicitly distinguishes the two events as "One abortion and one miscarriage" (Kapur ch. 24).
- Author: Manju Kapur — In Chapter 25, summarizing Virmati's isolation among her fellow MA students in Lahore, the narration again uses the exact phrase "She had had one abortion and one miscarriage" (Kapur ch. 25).
- Author: Manju Kapur — Within the characters' dialogue and Virmati's thoughts during the crisis, the procedure is also referred to indirectly through phrases such as "get rid of it," "deliverance from this unwanted burden," and "killing their child" (Kapur ch. 19).

#### 3.2 Who is told about the pregnancy and procedure/event (and when), and who is explicitly kept ignorant or not told
- Author: Manju Kapur — Swarna Lata (Virmati's hostel roommate) is told first, after Virmati returns to Lahore from her prep-leave visit to Amritsar having failed to contact Harish and having missed two months of menstruation (Kapur).
- Author: Manju Kapur — Decades later, Swarna Lata Sondhi confirms to Ida, "'Yes, she was pregnant,' said my old lady slowly, carefully. 'Though she only told me when she had to'" (Kapur ch. 19).

- Author: Manju Kapur — The male doctor (an old acquaintance of Miss Datta's family) is brought in at Miss Datta's house for an initial internal examination—estimating the pregnancy at about ten weeks—and performs the abortion two days later in Miss Datta's guest room (Kapur).
- Author: Manju Kapur — Ida (Virmati's daughter) learns about the pregnancy and abortion only after Virmati's death, when the elderly Swarna Lata Sondhi tells her during Ida's research (Kapur).
- Author: Manju Kapur — Harish (the Professor) is explicitly kept ignorant at the time: when Virmati returns to Amritsar on prep leave to tell him, he has gone away to his village for a month for his baby son's mundan without leaving an address, and Virmati fails to reach him through Kanhiya Lal (Kapur).
- Author: Manju Kapur — When Swarna asks Virmati about the father, Virmati admits, "He … he doesn't know," and Harish learns of the pregnancy and abortion only afterwards when Virmati returns to Amritsar and he asks, "Why didn't you at least inform me?" (Kapur ch. 19).
- Author: Manju Kapur — Virmati's parents (Kasturi and Suraj Prakash) and her natal family are explicitly kept completely ignorant: Virmati conceals her morning sickness at home, pretends she needs bangles because girls in Lahore wear them, lies that she donated the bangles to the British war effort, and Swarna later confirms to Ida that Virmati's family never knew because they would not have let her return to Lahore if they had (Kapur).
- Author: Manju Kapur — The RBSL hostel warden, college principal, fellow students, and practical examiner are kept ignorant: Virmati tells the warden she is leaving for prep leave simply because she will study better at home (Kapur).

#### 3.3 Verbatim passages showing how Virmati's inability to speak about the pregnancy, fear of shame, and physical/emotional pain are handled, who benefits from secrecy, and what it costs Virmati
- Author: Manju Kapur — On her inability to speak about the pregnancy, the narration shows Virmati unable even to name the condition privately in her thoughts: "she lay on the damp coolness of the thick khadi sheets ... aching with sadness for herself, for that thing inside her that she couldn't name for fear of making it more real" (Kapur ch. 19).

- Author: Manju Kapur — Even when she later meets Harish, Virmati suppresses her anger and grief: "Obviously not enough, rose to Virmati's lips, but she swallowed the words. - Author: Manju Kapur — Regarding her fear of shame, upon returning to Amritsar she resolves, "Whatever happened, she could not allow any further stigma to taint the family name" and dreads going to a hospital "silently, secretly, with her face veiled, her thighs open, for that little growing thing to be wrenched out of her" (Kapur ch. 19).
- Author: Manju Kapur — Discovering the doctor is a man deepens her humiliation: "now the thought of exposing herself clinically to a male made her grow hot with shame. What must his opinion of her be? She felt apprehension knot her stomach" (Kapur ch. 19).
- Author: Manju Kapur — Leaving Miss Datta's house after the examination, Virmati experiences total self-abasement: "Riding home, Virmati wished the road could swallow her up. Her nothingness was total. She felt severed from the body that was causing her friend's friends so much trouble. They were kind, they didn't say anything outright, but she knew herself to be a crawling worm dependent on other people's good wishes for survival" (Kapur ch. 19).
- Author: Manju Kapur — Regarding physical and emotional pain, upon discovering the pregnancy Virmati heaves yellowish bile and collapses with "sobs that racked her body as much as her vomiting had done, except that they lasted much longer" (Kapur ch. 19).
- Author: Manju Kapur — On the night before the abortion, she tests her endurance against physical pain through self-harm on the courtyard parapet: "She picked up the knife and slowly slashed at the soft skin on her calf. If she could brand her name there, that would mean she could survive the pain of tomorrow. But by the time she had carved out 'V there was too much blood for her to finish" (Kapur ch. 19).
- Author: Manju Kapur — During the internal exam, "Pain shot through Virmati's abdomen, and she involuntarily clenched her thighs together," and afterwards she endures raw wetness, tape on her wrist, abdominal aches, bicycle soreness, and wretched bleeding alongside "a deep emptiness inside her" (Kapur ch. 19).

- Author: Manju Kapur — Ida replies to Parvati Masi by citing Virmati's lifelong evasion: "'She never talked much about herself, Masi.' I feel obliged to defend myself. #### 4.2 How the 1947 Partition appears in the novel—what details reach Ida and the reader as second-hand fragments told by relatives, and what relatives emphasize or omit
- Author: Manju Kapur — Partition enters Ida's inquiry first through old Hindu newspapers covering the political collapse of March 1947 (Khizar Hayat Khan Tiwana's resignation, Master Tara Singh tearing the Muslim League flag, Governor's rule, and mass killings) and through a series of short, first-person testimonies from relatives and acquaintances (Kapur).
- Author: Manju Kapur — Swarna Lata Sondhi tells Ida in fragments about how Lahore residents never believed they would have to abandon their city until a Muslim friend secretly warned them, forcing them to flee arson and looting and abandon houses, furniture, books, and gardens; in Chapter 26 she recounts rooftops guarded with guns, making bombs, nightly communal battle cries, escaping just before her house was ransacked, and hearing refugees describe abductions, forced conversions, and starvation (Kapur).
- Author: Manju Kapur — Kailashnath recounts that Amritsar was fifty-one per cent Muslim out of 300,000 residents, claims Muslims were well prepared with bombs from 5 March onwards, describes making homemade kerosene-rag and gunpowder bombs, emptying their jewellery shop before it burned, losing his wife's family's cloth shop, citing "500,000 dead by the end of it all," and watching his father-in-law from Karachi waste away mourning lost property (Kapur ch. 26).
- Author: Manju Kapur — Gopinath describes vomiting at the station upon seeing a train covered in crusted blood with smashed windows and limbs hanging out, living as prisoners in their own homes, watching an uncle from Sultanpur sink into senility over what he lost, blaming the British as "Muslim-lovers" for drawing the border away from the River Ravi, yet ultimately admitting, "If we were stupid, greedy and uncivilized enough to allow religion to be used in this way, why blame them?" (Kapur ch. 26).
- Author: Manju Kapur — Kanhiya Lal recounts Amritsar burning nightly with red skies and smoke, mobs with lathis and swords, his family's safety as doctors who treated all wounded regardless of religion, feeling closer to Muslim friends than to fellow Hindus, and working in cholera-threatened refugee camps before leaving in 1947 (Kapur).
- Author: Manju Kapur — Indumati describes Amritsar opening every home as an ashram and turning angans into langars to feed refugees, attributes gruesome violence (beheadings, rapes, and mutilation) to Muslims who claimed retaliation for Hindu violence, and states that survivors buried the past in silence (Kapur).
- Author: Manju Kapur — Shakuntala offers only a brief three-sentence fragment reporting hearsay about her brother Somnath's death ("They say he was killed by some Muslims who had a grudge against him") and calling herself lucky to have a house and principalship waiting in Amritsar (Kapur ch. 26).
- Author: Manju Kapur — Parvati's husband describes Amritsar becoming a border city overnight with refugee processions fifty thousand strong and four camps (Govindgarh Fort, Sharifpura, Company Bagh, and Cantonment), refugees desperate to kill anyone not their own when relatives went missing, free food under Mridula Sarabhai, and bitterness over property exchanges (Kapur).
- Author: Manju Kapur — Relatives heavily emphasize material loss (abandoned or burned shops, houses, possessions), collective charitable hospitality in Amritsar's langars and camps, the sheer scale of death and horror, and (in several accounts, especially Kailashnath's and Indumati's) Muslim aggression or (in Gopinath's) British betrayal (Kapur).
- Author: Manju Kapur — Relatives omit or actively suppress specific first-hand accounts of atrocities committed by their own community: Indumati notes Muslim violence was claimed as "retaliation for what the Hindus were doing to them" without detailing Hindu actions, Parvati's husband states "we did our best to suppress the stories of atrocities" and dissuade vengeful killing, and Kailashnath and Gopinath cut off painful memories ("spare me your stories"; "It does no good to remember") while Indumati says they "never spoke of them either, because what was there to say?" (Kapur ch. 26).
- Author: Manju Kapur — Relatives' Partition fragments also completely omit Virmati's personal experiences during 1947—her moving Ganga's belongings into the dressing-room, conceiving in the courtyard tank, reconciling silently with Kasturi in the refugee langar, breaking open Ganga's locked cupboard to give away her clothes, and giving birth to Ida amid communal bloodshed—all of which appear separately in third-person narration after Nehru's Independence speech (Kapur).

#### 4.3 What the closing of Ida's frame says about her attempt to reconstruct and speak for her dead mother Virmati
- Author: Manju Kapur — In the Epilogue, Ida explains that her mother's death finally removes the oppressive shadow that kept her from investigating Virmati's life: "Now her shadow no longer threatens me. Without the hindrance of her presence, I can sink into her past and make it mine" (Kapur ch. 27).
- Author: Manju Kapur — Ida explicitly admits that her reconstruction relies on flawed, incomplete, and conflicting evidence rather than objective certainty: "In searching for a woman I could know, I have pieced together material from memories that were muddled, partial and contradictory" (Kapur ch. 27).
- Author: Manju Kapur — She acknowledges that the sites and texts she consulted could never give her a complete record: "The places I visited, the stuff I read tantalized me with fragments that I knew I would not be able fully to reconstruct" (Kapur ch. 27).
- Author: Manju Kapur — Consequently, Ida confesses that she actively invented and shaped the narrative herself to speak for her mother: "Instead, I imagined histories, rejecting the material that didn't fit, moulding ruthlessly the material that did" (Kapur ch. 27).
- Author: Manju Kapur — Ida frames the resulting book not as pure biography but as a healing creative bond forged out of her own intellect and emotion: "All through, I felt the excitement of discovery, the pleasure of fitting narratives into a discernible inheritance. This book weaves a connection between my mother and me, each word a brick in a mansion I made with my head and my heart" (Kapur ch. 27).
- Author: Manju Kapur — In the final two sentences, Ida encloses her mother inside the narrative she built so that she can finally lay Virmati's memory to rest and free herself from guilt and haunting: "Now live in it, Mama, and leave me be. Do not haunt me any more" (Kapur ch. 27).

The Politics of Female Silence in Manju Kapur's Select Novels (Paper title; about 30 pages of body text before Works Cited)

* Introduction and Roadmap
In the opening chapter of Manju Kapur's Difficult Daughters, Virmati's relatives cluster weeping around her funeral pyre while her daughter Ida looks on dry-eyed (Kapur). Denied even her own dying wishes—her body burned intact despite her explicit request to donate her organs and avoid mourning rituals—Virmati leaves behind a divorced, childless daughter burdened by guilt and longstanding estrangement (Kapur). Travelling back to the crowded ancestral house in Amritsar, Ida enters a noisy rush of aunts and uncles whose hospitality fills the rooms with chatter about old market prices for ghee, milk, and atta, yet who brush aside her questions about Virmati's past and urge her simply to forget and eat (Kapur). Looking at a faded sepia photograph of her mother at fifteen, Ida realizes that memory threatens to restore "the mother I knew, silent, brisk, and bad-tempered" (Kapur ch. 1). Across Kapur's fiction, households are loud—crowded with joint-family disputes, marriage arrangements, domestic instructions, and relatives' gossip—yet what each central woman most needs to say goes unsaid, or is spoken only to the reader.

That tension between domestic noise and female reticence raises the paper's central question: who decides what a woman in Kapur's fiction may say, to whom, and at what price? Approaching silence through the lens of politics shifts attention away from private shyness or individual temperament toward the power relations that organize speech—governing which desires, grievances, or histories become utterable and who benefits when they remain hidden. As the critical review section shows, existing scholarship on Kapur frequently approaches silence as a thematic symptom of oppression or a phase overcome by an emerging New Woman, leaving underexamined the machinery that produces and distributes it across households and institutions. Rather than treating silence as the mere absence of voice, the framework section that follows draws on feminist and postcolonial theory to build a working vocabulary for silence as a political category.

To trace those arrangements across Kapur's writing, this paper examines a six-novel corpus comprising the first six of her seven novels, published between 1998 and 2016: Difficult Daughters (1998), A Married Woman (2002), Home (2006), The Immigrant (2008), Custody (2011), and Brothers (2016). Born in Amritsar in 1948 (Akhtar; Rollason), educated at Dalhousie University in Halifax and Delhi University before teaching English at Miranda House for decades (Akhtar; Jha), Kapur turned to fiction late, publishing her first novel when she was close to fifty (Jha). The word "select" in this study's title therefore marks no arbitrary choice, but rather every novel she published prior to her recently released seventh novel, The Gallery (Jha). Set in Delhi, The Gallery follows Minal Sahni—who opens an art gallery in the garage of her Golf Links home—alongside Matti, a live-in domestic helper hired through Minal's husband's Nepali employee, as both women and their daughters navigate stark divisions of gender and class (Jha). Because The Gallery sits outside the 1998–2016 sequence, it remains the corpus's one consequential gap and receives fuller treatment in the counter-readings section; meanwhile, Kapur's edited collection Shaping the World: Women Writers on Themselves (Akhtar) and her published interviews remain outside the corpus and appear solely as context, never as evidence of what the novels do.

Across these six novels, the study tests the working claim that silence is not an absence of speech, but a distributed arrangement: it is assigned by family, community, law, and nation; bargained over and enforced as often by women as by men; used by women as shelter and strategy as well as suffered as loss; and carried by the novels' own forms in their frames, gaps, and endings. Rather than simply handing their heroines a voice, Kapur's narratives appear to measure what speech costs against what silence buys, declining to let either count as a clean victory. To keep that claim falsifiable so that the conclusion can evaluate what the textual evidence sustains, it is divided into three testable sub-claims: first, that female silence is institutionally assigned rather than purely personal; second, that it is negotiated within patriarchal constraints, including by women policing other women; and third, that the novels' narrative form itself registers and carries silence.

The paper advances in four movements. First, after situating the argument within existing criticism, it constructs a political vocabulary and passage-log method structured around six named types: imposed silence, punitive silence, strategic silence, complicit silence, unspeakable silence, and textual silence. Second, having built that vocabulary, the analysis reads the six novels across three sites where speech is regulated—the natal home, marriage, and the law or lineage's custody of mothers. Third, it tests that pattern against two pressures: first by examining how women enforce or navigate one another's silence through patriarchal bargaining, and then by reading the novels' frames, narrative gaps, and endings for formal silence. Fourth, it tests the argument against its own limits—especially class and subaltern boundaries highlighted by omitting The Gallery—and reports explicit verdicts on each sub-claim. Finally, the paper sets three boundaries on what it will not do: it will not claim that Kapur is a theorist of silence, will not treat her heroines as representative of Indian women, and will not read authorial interviews as proof of what the texts do.

* Silence as a Political Category: Concepts, Typology and Method
Earning the word "politics" in this study's title requires a compact working vocabulary capable of testing the three sub-claims outlined in the introduction: that female silence in Manju Kapur's fiction is institutionally assigned, negotiated within patriarchal constraints including among women, and carried by narrative form. Rather than surveying feminist and postcolonial theory at large, this section builds that vocabulary through four linked theoretical moves drawn from Michel Foucault, Audre Lorde, Adrienne Rich, Deniz Kandiyoti, Partha Chatterjee, and Urvashi Butalia—supplemented by a single representational distinction from Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak—before converting those concepts into a six-part coding typology and a balanced passage-log method.

Silence is produced, not found. In the chapter "The Incitement to Discourse" from The History of Sexuality, Volume 1, Michel Foucault dismantles the habit of treating speech and quietness as simple opposites, insisting that "There is no binary division to be made between what one says and what one does not say" (Foucault 15). Instead of viewing reticence as an empty void outside power, analysis must map "the different ways of not saying such things, how those who can and those who cannot speak of them are distributed, which type of discourse is authorized, or which form of discretion is required in either case" (Foucault 15). Tracing institutional boundaries of "tact and discretion" between speakers such as "parents and children" or "teachers and pupils" (Foucault 9), Foucault concludes: "There is not one but many silences, and they are an integral part of the strategies that underlie and permeate discourses" (Foucault 15). Silence—"the things one declines to say, or is forbidden to name, the discretion that is required between different speakers"—thus operates "alongside the things said, with them and in relation to them within over-all strategies" (Foucault 15). This means that, when reading Kapur, silence cannot be treated as private shyness or the mere absence of voice; every instance of withheld speech requires asking who benefits when a particular woman does not speak about a particular thing, and which household or institutional strategy her quietness serves.

Silence is unevenly priced. Whereas Foucault asks what strategies produce silence, Audre Lorde and Adrienne Rich measure the uneven cost borne by the woman who keeps or breaks it. In "The Transformation of Silence into Language and Action," delivered at the Modern Language Association's Lesbian and Literature Panel in 1977 (Lorde), Audre Lorde rejects the assumption that staying quiet purchases safety: "My silences had not protected me. Your silence will not protect you" (Lorde 41). Women may remain in "safe corners mute as bottles, and we will still be no less afraid" (Lorde 42) until "the weight of that silence will choke us" (Lorde 44). Yet Lorde refuses to present speech as a cost-free victory, warning that "the transformation of silence into language and action is an act of self-revelation, and that always seems fraught with danger" (Lorde 42)—exposing the speaker to "fear of contempt, of censure, or some judgment, or recognition, of challenge, of annihilation" (Lorde 42) alongside "the harsh light of scrutiny" and "pain" (Lorde 43). This means that, when reading Kapur, neither silence nor speech can be idealized as a clean triumph; the novels continually weigh what speaking out costs a woman in domestic security, marriage, or standing against what silent compliance costs her within herself. Paired with Lorde, Adrienne Rich's "Women and Honor: Some Notes on Lying" (in On Lies, Secrets, and Silence) connects silence directly to defensive concealment: "Lying is done with words, and also with silence" (Rich 186). Because women have historically been "rewarded for lying" (Rich 186) and "forced to lie, for survival, to men"—including authorities "who legally own us and our children" (Rich 189)—"discretion" (Rich 190) and acting out "The lie of the 'happy marriage,' of domesticity" (Rich 189) operate as survival tactics learned under dependence. Yet Rich stresses "the terrible negative power of the lie in relationships between women" (Rich 185), warning that deceit acquired under powerlessness can carry over into peer intimacy, where women undermine each other's reality or "gaslight each other" (Rich 190). This means that, when reading Kapur, female half-truths, evasions, and concealments must be read as survival techniques learned under material and marital dependence, while also asking what those necessary withholdings cost trust and solidarity between women.

Silence is negotiated. To explain how women themselves come to police other women's speech, Deniz Kandiyoti's "Bargaining with Patriarchy" turns from individual survival to generational power inside the household. Rejecting monolithic descriptions of male dominance, Kandiyoti argues that "Women strategize within a set of concrete constraints, which I identify as patriarchal bargains" (Kandiyoti 274), seeking "to maximize security and optimize life options" (Kandiyoti 274) under implicit rules offering "protection in exchange for submissiveness and propriety" (Kandiyoti 283). Under "classic patriarchy," which Kandiyoti locates across "North Africa, the Muslim Middle East (including Turkey, Pakistan, and Iran), and South and East Asia (specifically, India and China)" (Kandiyoti 278), a young bride enters a patrilocally extended household "as an effectively dispossessed individual" (Kandiyoti 279) subordinate not only to all men but also "to the more senior women, especially their mother-in-law" (Kandiyoti 278). Because "the deprivation and hardship she experiences as a young bride is eventually superseded by the control and authority she will have over her own subservient daughters-in-law" (Kandiyoti 279), aging women acquire an institutional stake in the family's rules, producing their "active collusion in the reproduction of their own subordination" (Kandiyoti 280). This means that, when reading Kapur, mothers, mothers-in-law, and senior wives who impose or enforce silence cannot be dismissed as simple villains; they act as participants in a patriarchal bargain whose terms tie senior female authority to keeping junior women quiet.

Silence has an address. Three Indian and postcolonial frames establish where and through whom these silences operate. First, in "The Nationalist Resolution of the Women's Question," Partha Chatterjee shows how nineteenth-century Indian nationalism divided social life "into ghar and bahir, the home and the world" (Chatterjee, "Nationalist" 238). While "The world is the external, the domain of the material" (Chatterjee, "Nationalist" 238) and "typically the domain of the male" (Chatterjee, "Nationalist" 238–39), "the home represents our inner spiritual self, our true identity" (Chatterjee, "Nationalist" 238) and "in its essence must remain unaffected by the profane activities of the material world — and woman is its representation" (Chatterjee, "Nationalist" 239). Charging women with preserving that inner domain "bound them to a new, and yet entirely legitimate, subordination" (Chatterjee, "Nationalist" 248)—a discourse in which, as Chatterjee notes in his companion essay, "women do not speak here" (Chatterjee, "Colonialism" 632). This means that, when reading Kapur, the home is never an apolitical private refuge; it is the historical address where female respectability, modesty, and speech are most tightly regulated. Second, Urvashi Butalia's The Other Side of Silence: Voices from the Partition of India locates that domestic silence within historical violence, showing how Partition atrocities—including abduction, rape, and intra-family killings committed to protect "the honour of the community" (Butalia 359)—were absorbed into both "historical silence" and "familial silence" (Butalia 358). Families hid disappeared women as "something to be ashamed of" (Butalia 134) or rejected recovered survivors as "soiled" and "polluted" (Butalia 162), creating a condition in which, "For women as a group, then, their only collectivity lay in silence" (Butalia 330). Equally crucial for reading narrative frames, Butalia documents how male relatives "tended to take over the interview, inadvertently or otherwise, making women lapse into a sort of silence" (Butalia 15), and emphasizes that recovering women's accounts requires attending to "the hidden nuance, the half-said thing, the silences which are sometimes more eloquent than speech" (Butalia 16). This means that, when reading Kapur—especially Difficult Daughters—family secrecy must be read alongside Partition's public erasure, and every relayed testimony must be examined for what relatives and collectors omit or reshape. Third, Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak's "Can the Subaltern Speak?" supplies one essential analytical distinction by separating "two senses of representation" that are "related but irreducibly discontinuous": "representation as 'speaking for', as in politics, and representation as 're-presentation', as in art or philosophy" (Spivak 70), or the "contrast, say, between a proxy and a portrait" (Spivak 71). Spivak's sharper claim—that "The subaltern as female cannot be heard or read" (Spivak 104)—applies to "men and women among the illiterate peasantry, the tribals, the lowest strata of the urban subproletariat" (Spivak 78) rather than to Kapur's educated, urban middle-class protagonists, and is therefore held for the counter-readings section to ask whose silences the novels leave unwritten. This means that, when reading Kapur, any surrogate speech—whether a father arranging a marriage, a lawyer arguing in court, or a daughter like Ida reconstructing her dead mother's life—must be scrutinized for how artistic portraiture can mask the political act of speaking for another woman.

While Elaine Showalter's adaptation of Edwin and Shirley Ardener's "muted group" model usefully observes that "dominant groups control the forms or structures in which consciousness can be articulated," compelling women into a "double-voiced discourse" spoken through "the language of the dominant order" (Showalter 200–01), testing Kapur's six novels requires a sharper, strictly defined coding scheme rather than a general theory of mutedness. To ensure consistent tracking across every analysis section, the study defines six named categories of silence—each introduced in one clause and cited exclusively by name, never by number. Imposed silence occurs when an authority orders quiet or arranges that a woman cannot speak, including being spoken for by a father, a lawyer, or a narrator. Punitive silence occurs when a woman speaks or acts and is then not spoken to or not spoken of. Strategic silence occurs when a woman withholds speech to protect herself, someone she loves, or a plan. Complicit silence occurs when a woman keeps, or makes another woman keep, a silence that protects the household's honour. Unspeakable silence occurs when no available language exists for the thing, whether desire, abuse, the experience of Partition, or same-sex love. Textual silence occurs when the narration itself withholds speech or information in the frame, the narrative gap, or the ending.
